newsitem.title: USA: Canada's Sergio urges arbitration in US salmon spat.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Sergio urges arbitration in US salmon spat.

text.p: Canadian Trade Minister Sergio Marchi said on Wednesday he hoped the military alliance with the United States can be separated from the salmon fishing squabble between the two neighbours.

"We are all hopeful that the two can be separated ultimately," Sergio told reporters after meeting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky. It was their first meeting since Sergio became trade minister.
Sergio reiterated Canada's desire to put the issue to binding arbitration since bilateral negotiations on how to manage dwindling salmon stocks failed to produce an agreement.

"We are prepared to put the facts on the table, put ourselves at a distance from that table and allow the facts to come to the table, and for decisions to be made obviously in the best interest of conservation," he said.

Sergio said Barshefsky was sensitive to the the issue particularly since the salmon squabble spilled over into the military alliance when British Columbia Premier Glen Clark announced in May that his province was cancelling the lease on an underwater military test range used by the United States.
The Canadian Maritime Experimental test range at Nanoose Bay on Canada's Pacific coast is used by U.S. submarines as a torpedo test range under a Canada-U.S. defence agreement.

Canada and the United States have been holding sporadic talks for the past few months on how to divide dwindling Pacific salmon. But the two sides failed to reach agreement before the start of this year's season.

In May, Canada announced it would begin enforcing requirements for U.S. boats fishing in Canadian waters to report to Canadian authories and the Canadian coast guard temporarily seized four U.S. fishing boats.

The two sides described the Sergio-Barshefsky meeting as a "get-to-know-you" session. But the trade chiefs discussed a number of bilateral trade issues, including U.S. concerns about Canadian exports of wheat and wool suits into U.S. markets. The two also discussed the North American Free Trade Agreement and Canada's concerns about the so-called Helms-Burton law aimed at discouraging foreign investment in Cuba.
